"'''Windy'''" is a [[pop music|pop]] song written by [[Ruthann Friedman]] and recorded by [[the Association]].<ref name=pc37>{{cite web|url=https://digital.library.unt.edu/ark:/67531/metadc19796/m1/ |title=Show 37 – The Rubberization of Soul: The great pop music renaissance. [Part 3] : UNT Digital Library |publisher=Digital.library.unt.edu |year=1969 |work=[[Pop Chronicles]] |format=audio |access-date=2011-04-14}}</ref> The song reached No. 1 on the [[Billboard Hot 100|''Billboard'' Hot 100]] in July 1967, becoming the group's second U.S. No. 1 hit following "[[Cherish (The Association song)|Cherish]]" in 1966. ''Billboard'' ranked the record as the [[Billboard Year-End Hot 100 singles of 1967|No. 4 song for 1967]]. 

The lead vocals were sung primarily by guitarist and new band member [[Larry Ramos]] along with vocalist Russ Giguere (both would sing lead together in the band's last Top 40 hit "[[Time for Livin' (The Association song)|Time for Livin']]{{-"}}).  Ramos, who was of [[Philippines|Filipino]] descent,<REF>[https://www.latimes.com/local/obituaries/la-me-passings-20140506-story.html LAtimes.com "Passings - Larry Ramos" May 5, 2014.  Retrieved Feb. 5, 2024.]</REF> was one of the few [[Asian-American]] lead singers at the time to have a number one hit single.

"Windy" is a pop song written by Ruthann Friedman and recorded by the Association. The song reached No. 1 on the Billboard Hot 100 in July 1967, becoming the group's second U.S. No. 1 hit following "Cherish" in 1966. Billboard ranked the record as the No. 4 song for 1967. 

The lead vocals were sung primarily by guitarist and new band member Larry Ramos along with vocalist Russ Giguere (both would sing lead together in the band's last Top 40 hit "Time for Livin'{{-"}}).  Ramos, who was of Filipino descent,<REF>[https://www.latimes.com/local/obituaries/la-me-passings-20140506-story.html LAtimes.com "Passings - Larry Ramos" May 5, 2014.  Retrieved Feb. 5, 2024.]</REF> was one of the few Asian-American lead singers at the time to have a number one hit single.

sections.heading: Composition
Recording
sections.wikitext:
The process of recording the vocals was exhausting. The session started in the early afternoon and ended at 6:30 a.m. the next day, and the group then took an 8:30 a.m. flight to a live performance in [[Virginia]].<ref name="songfacts">{{cite web|title=Windy|url=http://www.songfacts.com/detail.php?id=1874|access-date=2015-07-01|work=Songfacts.com}}</ref> The band was so tired of recording that producer Bones Howe gathered everyone in the studio to sing the track's ending, including songwriter Ruthann Friedman.<ref name="songfacts" /><ref>{{Citation|title=Windy - The Association {{!}} Song Info {{!}} AllMusic|url=https://www.allmusic.com/song/windy-mt0004442106|language=en|access-date=2021-03-23}}</ref>

Because of the poor sales of the Association's last album [[Renaissance (The Association album)|''Renaissance'']], on which the group performed all of the songs, Howe recruited session musicians (later known as [[The Wrecking Crew (music)|the Wrecking Crew]]) for "Windy" and the rest of the ''[[Insight Out]]'' album in order to achieve a radio-friendly sound. The identity of the musicians who played on the final version of the single is uncertain because the song was recorded during several sessions.
sections.text:
The process of recording the vocals was exhausting. The session started in the early afternoon and ended at 6:30 a.m. the next day, and the group then took an 8:30 a.m. flight to a live performance in Virginia. The band was so tired of recording that producer Bones Howe gathered everyone in the studio to sing the track's ending, including songwriter Ruthann Friedman.

Because of the poor sales of the Association's last album Renaissance, on which the group performed all of the songs, Howe recruited session musicians (later known as the Wrecking Crew) for "Windy" and the rest of the Insight Out album in order to achieve a radio-friendly sound. The identity of the musicians who played on the final version of the single is uncertain because the song was recorded during several sessions.

sections.heading: Notable cover versions
sections.wikitext: *Later in 1967, an instrumental version by jazz [[guitarist]] [[Wes Montgomery]] became his highest-charting Hot 100 hit when it peaked at No. 44.<ref>{{cite book |title=  Joel Whitburn's Top Pop Singles, 14th Edition: 1955-2012 |last=Whitburn |first=Joel |authorlink=Joel Whitburn |year=2013 |publisher=Record Research |page=587}}</ref> It also reached No. 10 on the ''Billboard'' [[Adult Contemporary (chart)|Easy Listening]] chart.<ref>{{cite book |title= Top Adult Contemporary: 1961-2001|last=Whitburn |first=Joel |authorlink=Joel Whitburn |year=2002 |publisher=Record Research |page=173}}</ref> Andy Williams also recorded the song.
sections.text: *Later in 1967, an instrumental version by jazz guitarist Wes Montgomery became his highest-charting Hot 100 hit when it peaked at No. 44. It also reached No. 10 on the Billboard Easy Listening chart. Andy Williams also recorded the song.
